sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source consists of a NE-SW striking, N-dipping, reverse fault system located in the northern Ligurian Sea, a few kilometers off the Italy-France coastline. This is one of the most seismically active areas in the western Mediterranean.
The northern Ligurian margin is characterized by a narrow (0.2-2.0 km-wide) continental shelf extending between Nice and Imperia) and by a 20 km-wide, steep continental slope (with an average slope of 8Â° and a maximum slope of 20Â°) down to 2,600 m depth. The continental slope is affected by numerous scarps due to sediment failures and sub-marine landslides (e.g. Migeon et al., 2011).
Geophysical surveys have shown that the crust thins down from 45 km under the Argentera Massif (about 40 km away from the coast) to 20 km beneath the coastline, and to less than 10 km beneath the northern margin of the Ligurian Basin (Thouvenot et al., 2007). This margin shows typical features of a rifted continental margin, and the Ligurian Basin is thought to be developed in a back-arc context (e.g. Doglioni et al., 1997).
Having noted that the margin is affected by shallow, south-dipping normal faults but also by compressional earthquakes at depth, Chaumillion et al. (1994) suggested that the margin is the result of a flexural mechanism. This hypothesis was in open contrast with contemporary interpretations which maintained that the northern Ligurian margin is a typical passive margin (Rollet et al., 2002). Later on Bigot-Cormier et al. (2004) proposed an interpretative deformation model of post-Messinian tectonics in the north-Ligurian margin between Antibes and Imperia, stressing the different role played by south-dipping normal faults and north-dipping thrusts. Also Foeken et al. (2003) and Foeken (2004) explained the long-term uplift of the Ligurian Alps by south-verging thrusting.
Based on the interpretation of high-resolution multi-beam bathymetric data collected during the MALISAR surveys (2006, 2007, 2008), Larroque et al. (2009, 2011, 2012) identified a large number of submarine failures along the northern margin of the Ligurian basin. The observed morphological features attest to recent and significant deformation. These data allowed them to identify the Ligurian Fault System, a transpressional system of Plio-Quaternary faults, consistent with the present-day kinematics (Larroque et al., 2009, 2011, 2012).
Near the southwestern border of the Ligurian Fault System Larroque et al. (2011) reported evidence of Quaternary activity along the so-called "Marcel Fault", a N60Â°E, 10 km-long scarp at the foot of the continental slope. The Marcel Fault scarp is 30 m-high at its steepest part. According to the same investigators, near the northeastern border of the Ligurian Fault System, off the Imperia coastline, the southeastern flank of a large elongated promontory is bound by a network of N60Â°E faults. This 40 km-long ridge lies above the continental slope and is referred to as the Imperia Promontory. At the top of the promontory, the Messinian erosion surface and at least two unconformities are tilted northwestward. Larroque et al. (2011) proposed a long-term uplift rate of 0.40-0.53 mm/y for this structure during the Plio-Quaternary.
Larroque et al. (2009) used CGPS data to detect consistent shortening in the N-S direction. The shortening rate across the Ligurian margin is of 0.4-0.8 mm/y.
Historical and instrumental catalogues (Guidoboni et al., 2007; Rovida et al., 2011) show a number of intermediate-size (4.5 < Mw < 5.0) to damaging earthquakes surrounding the area, but also the key damaging earthquakes (from west to east) that occurred on 23 February 1818 (Mw 5.8), 26 May 1831 (Mw 5.5), and 29 December 1854 (Mw 5.8), plus the destructive 23 February 1887 (Mw 6.6) event. The latter earthquake was accompanied by a sizeable tsunami.
Earthquake focal mechanisms along both the onshore and the offshore front confirm that the area is undergoing N-S to NW-SE compression, as shown specifically by the 21 April 1995, Mw 4.7, Ventimiglia earthquake (e.g. Bethoux et al., 1992; Courboulex et al., 1998; Larroque et al., 2009).
A segment of this Composite Source has been associated with the 1887 earthquake as an Individual Source.
The strike of this Source was chosen according to that of the Ligurian Fault System. The dip was chosen in accordance with subsurface data. The rake was assumed to be representative of pure thrusting, based on geological observations and on the stress field retrieved from focal mechanisms. The minimum and maximum source depth were based on subsurface data and on geometrical considerations concerning the thrust geometry. The slip rate was inferred from geological evidence of long-term uplift from various sources.

pictures.t: Seismic profiles interpreted by Larroque et al. [2011]
pictures.c: Two seismic profiles across the Imperia Promontory (top) and their interpretation (bottom). Notice the tilting northwestward of the Messinian erosion surface, interpreted as a result of the growth of the anticline (from Larroque et al. [2011]).

pictures.t: Seismic lines across the Ligurian margin and structural map
pictures.c: Interpretation of seismic lines across the Ligurian margin outlining the presence of shallow, south-dipping normal faults. The presence of compressional earthquakes at depth suggests the margin is the result of a flexural mechanism (from Chaumillion et al. [1994]).

Interpretative deformation model of post-Messinian tectonics in north-Ligurian margin between Antibes and Imperia. The model underlines the different roles between south-dipping normal faults and north-dipping thrusts (from Bigot-Cormier et al. [2004]).
